summary: IMAP4rev2 lets an email client access and manage messages kept on a server, treating remote mailboxes like local folders. It includes creating, deleting and renaming mailboxes, checking for new messages, flags, searching and selective fetching, and it supports offline clients that resynchronize later. It does not cover sending mail, which is left to a submission protocol such as the one in RFC 6409.

eli5.summary: IMAP lets you read your email from any device while the messages stay on a big mail computer, like keeping your letters in a post office box. This is the newest version of those rules.

questions: how does imap access mailboxes on a server
what is the difference between imap4rev1 and imap4rev2
what is a uid in imap
subtitle: The current rules for reading and managing email that stays on a server, folded together from IMAP4rev1 and its popular extensions.

tldr.problem: People read mail from several devices, so the messages have to stay on a server while clients browse, search, flag, move and delete them as if the folders were local. IMAP4rev1 (RFC 3501) had grown a long tail of extensions and some problematic features.
tldr.mechanism: IMAP4rev2 is a text protocol over a reliable stream. A client sends tagged commands, and the server answers with untagged data and a tagged OK, NO or BAD. Messages are addressed by sequence number or by a unique identifier (UID), and the connection moves through four states.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9051 obsoletes RFC 3501. It builds the widely used extensions (IDLE, MOVE, UIDPLUS, ESEARCH, ENABLE and others) into the base protocol, adds UTF-8 and 64-bit sizes, and updates the TLS guidance.

today: RFC 9051 is a Proposed Standard from August 2021 and obsoletes RFC 3501 (IMAP4rev1). The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What IMAP4rev2 Is and Is Not
sections.content:
IMAP4rev2 lets a client access and manipulate electronic mail messages on a server. Remote mailboxes (message folders) behave in a way that is functionally equivalent to local folders, and an offline client can resynchronize with the server later. The operations include creating, deleting and renaming mailboxes, checking for new messages, removing messages permanently, setting and clearing flags, searching, and selectively fetching message attributes, texts and portions of them.

The protocol does not send mail. The RFC says posting mail is handled by a mail submission protocol such as the one in RFC 6409. It also describes itself as written for the implementor of a client or server, so it is a reference rather than a tutorial, and command syntax must be taken from the formal syntax in Section 9, not from the command descriptions alone.

IMAP4rev2 is designed to be upwards compatible from IMAP4rev1 (RFC 3501), IMAP2 and the unpublished IMAP2bis. It assumes a reliable data stream such as TCP. Over TCP, a server listens on port 143 (cleartext) or port 993 (Implicit TLS).

Every interaction is a line ending in CRLF. A client prefixes each command with a tag such as A0001. Data the server sends is prefixed with an asterisk (untagged), a request for more client input is prefixed with +, and the final result of a command carries the command's tag with OK (success), NO (failure) or BAD (protocol error).
sections.eli5: IMAP is a set of rules for a mail program to ask a mail server, 'show me my messages' or 'put this one in that folder'. Sending mail is a different job with different rules.

sections.title: Messages, Numbers and Flags
sections.content:
Each message can be named in two ways. A message sequence number is its relative position from 1 to the number of messages in the mailbox, ordered by ascending UID. These numbers shift: when a message is expunged, every later message's number drops by one. A unique identifier (UID) is an unsigned non-zero 32-bit value, assigned in strictly ascending order as messages are added, though not necessarily contiguous.

A UID only makes sense together with the mailbox's UIDVALIDITY value. If UIDs from an earlier session fail to persist, the server MUST send a larger UIDVALIDITY, which tells a client to throw away its cached UIDs. The combination of mailbox name, UIDVALIDITY and UID must refer to a single message forever, and the message's internal date, RFC822.SIZE, envelope, body structure and texts must never change. A mailbox also has a UIDNEXT value, the predicted UID of the next message.

Each message has flags: system flags that begin with a backslash and keywords defined by the server. The defined system flags are \Seen, \Answered, \Flagged, \Deleted and \Draft, while \Recent is deprecated. Servers SHOULD also support the keywords $Forwarded, $MDNSent, $Junk, $NotJunk and $Phishing. A message also has an internal date (when the server received it), a size, an envelope (a parsed form of the RFC 5322 header) and a body structure (a parsed MIME structure).

Mailbox names are encoded in Net-Unicode. The case-insensitive name INBOX means the primary mailbox of the user. Namespaces separate the user's personal mailboxes, other users' mailboxes and shared mailboxes.
sections.eli5: Every letter in your mailbox gets a number for where it sits in the pile, and that number changes when letters are removed. It also gets a permanent serial number that never changes, plus little stickers like 'read' or 'important'.

sections.title: The Four Connection States
sections.content:
A connection is always in one of four states, and most commands are only valid in certain states. Using a command in the wrong state is a protocol error and gets a BAD or NO.

  • Not Authenticated: the client MUST supply credentials before most commands are allowed. This is where a connection starts, unless it was pre-authenticated.
  • Authenticated: the client is known, and MUST select a mailbox before commands that affect messages are allowed.
  • Selected: a mailbox has been selected, so commands on messages work.
  • Logout: the connection is ending.

The server greeting decides the first step: an OK greeting leads to Not Authenticated, a PREAUTH greeting goes straight to Authenticated, and a BYE greeting rejects the connection. A client that wants to leave SHOULD issue LOGOUT rather than just closing the connection, and the server MUST send an untagged BYE before its tagged OK. Only one mailbox can be selected at a time per connection, so using several mailboxes at once needs several connections.
sections.eli5: It is like entering a building: first you are at the front door, then you are signed in, then you walk into one particular room, and finally you leave.

sections.title: Data Formats and Pipelining
sections.content:
Commands and responses are text built from atoms, numbers, strings, parenthesized lists and NIL. A string is a quoted string, a synchronizing literal or a non-synchronizing literal. A literal is written as an octet count in braces, such as {342}, followed by the raw octets. A client sending a synchronizing literal MUST wait for the server's + continuation first, while a non-synchronizing literal (written {342+}) needs no wait but MUST NOT be larger than 4096 octets. Quoted strings are UTF-8, and servers MUST accept UTF-8 in quoted strings that contain no NUL, CR or LF.

Messages are chosen with a sequence set such as 5:50 or a list of numbers, where an asterisk stands for the largest number in use. A UID set is similar but cannot contain the asterisk.

A client MAY send a new command before the previous one completes (pipelining). The catch is ambiguity. If a command could change the results of another, the server MUST run them in order. Because untagged EXPUNGE responses renumber messages, a client that sends any command other than FETCH, STORE or SEARCH MUST wait for its completion before sending a command that uses sequence numbers. The RFC lists FETCH + STORE + SEARCH + NOOP as valid and COPY + COPY as invalid.
sections.eli5: The words in IMAP are plain text. If you want to send a big blob, you first say how long it is, then you send it. You can also line up several questions in a row, but not if the answer to one would change the next.

sections.title: Connecting Securely and Logging In
sections.content:
The CAPABILITY command lists what the server supports, and the reply MUST include IMAP4rev2. Names starting with AUTH= list supported SASL mechanisms. On cleartext ports, implementations MUST support STARTTLS and LOGINDISABLED, and everyone MUST support AUTH=PLAIN on both cleartext and Implicit TLS ports.

STARTTLS upgrades a cleartext connection to TLS. After TLS starts, the client MUST discard cached capabilities and SHOULD ask again, which defends against an attacker who altered the list before the upgrade. Servers MUST also guard against plaintext command injection by treating any extra data in the same TCP buffer as the start of the TLS handshake or discarding it.

AUTHENTICATE runs a SASL exchange in which the server sends base64 challenges after a + and the client answers with base64 lines, or a line with a single asterisk to cancel. LOGIN sends a plaintext password, SHOULD only be a last resort, and a client MUST NOT send it if LOGINDISABLED is advertised. A server MUST implement a configuration that refuses plaintext password mechanisms unless TLS or some other protection is in place.

The ENABLE command, valid only in the authenticated state before a mailbox is selected, lets a client opt in to extensions that change what the server may send. Once enabled, an extension stays on until the connection closes.
sections.eli5: Before you tell the mail server your password, you first put on a secret code so nobody listening can hear it. Then you prove who you are, and only then does the server let you in.

sections.title: Working with Mailboxes and Messages
sections.content:
In the authenticated state, a client manages mailboxes with SELECT and EXAMINE (open for read-write or read-only), CREATE, DELETE, RENAME, SUBSCRIBE, UNSUBSCRIBE, LIST, NAMESPACE, STATUS and APPEND. A successful SELECT makes the server report the mailbox flags, the message count (EXISTS), UIDNEXT and UIDVALIDITY. STATUS reports counts such as MESSAGES, UNSEEN and DELETED for another mailbox, but MUST NOT be used to check for new messages in the selected one.

In the selected state, FETCH retrieves message data such as FLAGS, ENVELOPE, BODYSTRUCTURE and BODY[...] sections, and may fetch just a byte range. The macros ALL, FAST and FULL bundle common sets of items. STORE changes flags with FLAGS, +FLAGS or -FLAGS. SEARCH returns matches in an ESEARCH response, with result options MIN, MAX, ALL, COUNT and SAVE, and servers MUST support the UTF-8 and US-ASCII character sets.

Deleting takes two steps. Setting \Deleted only marks a message, and EXPUNGE removes it for good and reports each removal as an untagged EXPUNGE response. CLOSE expunges silently and returns to the authenticated state, while UNSELECT leaves without removing anything. COPY and MOVE send messages to another mailbox and a server MUST NOT create the destination automatically, though it hints with [TRYCREATE]. A MOVE acts like copy, mark deleted and expunge, but without the intermediate states. The UID prefix makes FETCH, STORE, COPY, MOVE, SEARCH and EXPUNGE work with UIDs.

IDLE lets the server push changes in real time instead of the client polling. The client ends it by sending DONE, and is advised to reissue it at least every 29 minutes. A server inactivity autologout timer, if there is one, MUST be at least 30 minutes after authentication.
sections.eli5: Opening a folder is like taking out a stack of letters. You can look at them, put stickers on them, move them or throw them away. Throwing away is a two-step thing, first 'mark for the bin', then 'empty the bin'.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
IMAP traffic, including the mail itself, travels in the clear unless protection is negotiated through the Implicit TLS port, STARTTLS, a SASL security layer, or another mechanism. Implementations MUST support TLS 1.2 or newer, with TLS 1.3 RECOMMENDED. With TLS 1.2 they MUST implement TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256. The client MUST check the server hostname against the certificate, and the RFC follows RFC 8314 on using TLS for email access.

The server MUST implement TLS on an Implicit TLS port, and if it also listens on a cleartext port it MUST allow STARTTLS there. Clients SHOULD try ports 993 and 143 concurrently by default. Clients MUST implement both approaches.

Because a cleartext attacker could inject responses, clients SHOULD ignore most responses before authentication other than CAPABILITY and status responses. They also SHOULD ignore the ALERT response code until TLS or a confidential SASL layer is in place. The PREAUTH greeting skips STARTTLS entirely, so it SHOULD only be used on connections already protected, and clients that require TLS MUST close the connection if it appears on an unprotected port.

Servers SHOULD NOT reveal whether the user name or the password was wrong, SHOULD limit or delay failed attempts, and MUST NOT list other users' mailboxes the current user has no list access to. The MD5 value that can appear in a body structure only exposes a Content-MD5 header and is not used cryptographically.
sections.eli5: Mail is like postcards unless you put it in a locked box. The rules say to always use the locked box, check that the box really belongs to your mail server, and not tell strangers which part of your login was wrong.

sections.title: What Changed from IMAP4rev1
sections.content:
Appendix E lists 30 changes from RFC 3501. The main one is that several separate extensions are now part of the base protocol, including NAMESPACE, UNSELECT, UIDPLUS, ESEARCH, SEARCHRES, ENABLE, IDLE, SASL-IR, LIST-EXTENDED, LIST-STATUS, MOVE and LITERAL-.

The other changes include:

  • Support for 64-bit message and body part sizes.
  • A SEARCH command that must return ESEARCH, with the old SEARCH response deprecated.
  • UTF-8 allowed in mailbox names and message headers, with modified UTF-7 only needed for IMAP4rev1 compatibility.
  • The CHECK command removed, since clients should use NOOP, and LSUB deprecated in favor of LIST (SUBSCRIBED).
  • The RFC822, RFC822.HEADER and RFC822.TEXT FETCH items deprecated in favor of BODY[] variants.
  • DIGEST-MD5 replaced by SCRAM-SHA-256, and TLS guidance modernized.

A server can advertise both IMAP4rev1 and IMAP4rev2. In that case a client uses ENABLE IMAP4rev2 to opt in to the newer behavior. Appendix F recommends, but does not require, the QRESYNC and CONDSTORE extensions of RFC 7162 and the OBJECTID extension.
sections.eli5: This new edition takes all the handy add-ons people had been bolting onto the old IMAP and builds them into the main rule book, and throws out a few bits that caused trouble.
